topic: Strange borders: the Irish speed sign and five more that make no sense
hook: Your speed sign flips from miles to kilometres on a road that never changes.
title: 6 Absurd Borders, Ending in India's Weirdest
description:
Drive across the Irish border and your speed sign changes from miles to kilometres, with no gate and no guard. This countdown visits six real borders that make no sense: a German village inside Switzerland, a Spanish town in France, a piece of America you reach through Canada, a whole country inside another, and India's strangest enclave of all.

#borders #geography #strangefacts

chapters.title: The countdown and what is next

scenes.narration: Your speed sign flips from miles to kilometres on a road that never changes.
scenes.headline: The Sign That Flips

scenes.narration: That is border number six on today's list, and it is the most normal one. Everything after it gets stranger.
scenes.headline: Six Strange Borders

scenes.narration: We will visit a village stuck inside another country, and a town that Spain owns in the middle of France.
scenes.headline: Stuck Inside Countries

scenes.narration: Then a patch of America you can only reach by driving through Canada, and a whole country hidden inside another.
scenes.headline: Reached Through Canada

scenes.narration: And at the very end, an Indian border so strange that one little plot sat inside three layers of countries.
scenes.headline: India's Strangest

scenes.narration: Stay till the end, because that last one is real, it is in India, and it ended only a few years ago.
scenes.headline: It Ended In 2015

scenes.narration: Number six. Drive north on the road between Dundalk and Newry, and nothing looks different at first.
scenes.headline: Number Six: Ireland

scenes.narration: There is no gate, no guard and no passport check. The road, the fields and the weather all stay the same.
scenes.headline: No Gate, No Guard

scenes.narration: But watch the speed signs. In the Republic of Ireland, they are in kilometres per hour.
scenes.headline: Republic: km/h

scenes.narration: Cross into Northern Ireland, part of the United Kingdom, and the same kind of sign now means miles per hour.
scenes.headline: North: mph

scenes.narration: So a number on a sign can be a different speed, depending on which side of an invisible line you are on.
scenes.headline: Same Number, New Speed

scenes.narration: A limit of 100 in the Republic is about 62 miles per hour. Your speedometer might show either unit, so check.
scenes.headline: 100 km/h Is 62 mph

scenes.narration: Distances change too. Road signs in the Republic count kilometres to the next town, and in the north they count miles.
scenes.headline: Distances Change Too

scenes.narration: Locals cross this line every day to work, shop and visit family, often without noticing they have changed countries.
scenes.headline: Crossed Every Day

scenes.narration: The border runs about five hundred kilometres across the island, and many small roads cross it, with nothing to mark them.
scenes.headline: About 500 Kilometres

scenes.narration: Often the only clue is the speed sign, a number that quietly changes its meaning.
scenes.headline: The Only Clue

scenes.narration: So that is number six: a border you can see only in the units on the sign. Now it gets stranger.
scenes.headline: A Border In Units

scenes.narration: Next, a village that is German, but you cannot reach Germany from it without driving through Switzerland.
scenes.headline: Next: A Trapped Village

scenes.narration: Number five. Büsingen am Hochrhein is a German village, and it is completely surrounded by Switzerland.
scenes.headline: Number Five: Büsingen

scenes.narration: Look at the map and you see a small German pocket, with Switzerland all around it.
scenes.headline: A German Pocket

scenes.narration: To reach the rest of Germany by road, you must drive through Switzerland first.
scenes.headline: Drive Through Switzerland

scenes.narration: Because of an old border deal, the village sits inside the Swiss customs area, which is the same as Switzerland for trade.
scenes.headline: Swiss Customs Area

scenes.narration: Shops there widely accept Swiss francs, even though Germany uses the euro.
scenes.headline: Francs In Germany

scenes.narration: Even the car number plates are special. Cars from the village carry the letters B, Ü, S, which no other German town uses.
scenes.headline: Plates Marked BÜS

scenes.narration: Swiss and German rules mix together here, so a small village has to follow two systems at once.
scenes.headline: Two Systems At Once

scenes.narration: A German village in Switzerland sounds odd, but wait: the next one is a Spanish town inside France.
scenes.headline: Spain Inside France

scenes.narration: And it is there because of one word in a treaty from the sixteen hundreds.
scenes.headline: One Word In A Treaty

scenes.narration: Number four. Llívia is a Spanish town, but it sits inside France, about one and a half kilometres from the Spanish border.
scenes.headline: Number Four: Llívia

scenes.narration: In 1659, Spain and France signed the Treaty of the Pyrenees, and Spain gave France a group of villages.
scenes.headline: The 1659 Treaty

scenes.narration: Llívia was officially a town, not a village. So the treaty did not cover it, and it stayed Spanish.
scenes.headline: Town, Not Village

scenes.narration: That one tiny difference in a word still shapes the map today, more than three centuries later.
scenes.headline: Still On The Map

scenes.narration: A short road, called the neutral road, joins Llívia to Spain, and it passes through French land.
scenes.headline: The Neutral Road

scenes.narration: Llívia even has one of Europe's oldest pharmacies, now a museum you can visit.
scenes.headline: An Old Pharmacy

scenes.narration: So you can have lunch in France, drive a few minutes, and eat dessert in Spain, without leaving the mountains.
scenes.headline: Lunch, Then Dessert

scenes.narration: Two countries, one valley, and a town that exists on the Spanish side only because of a legal word.
scenes.headline: Two Countries, One Valley

scenes.narration: But our next one is a corner of America above the line, and a mapmaker's mistake put it there.
scenes.headline: A Mapmaker's Mistake

scenes.narration: Number three. The Northwest Angle is part of Minnesota, but it hangs off the top of the state, north of the main border.
scenes.headline: Number Three: The Angle

scenes.narration: Look at the 48 mainland states. This is the only place in them north of the 49th parallel.
scenes.headline: North Of The 49th

scenes.narration: To reach it by road, you have to drive through Canada, and then enter America again on the other side.
scenes.headline: Drive Through Canada

scenes.narration: Or you can take a boat across Lake of the Woods, which is how many visitors actually arrive.
scenes.headline: Or Take A Boat

scenes.narration: The reason is a mapmaking mistake. In 1783, the treaty after the American Revolution used a map that was wrong.
scenes.headline: The Wrong Map

scenes.narration: The treaty said the border would go to the northwestern point of Lake of the Woods, and then due west.
scenes.headline: Due West, Supposedly

scenes.narration: But the real lake and rivers did not line up with the map, and later talks left this piece on the American side.
scenes.headline: Lake Did Not Match

scenes.narration: So a bit of the USA is stuck up there, with forests, fishing lodges and water all around.
scenes.headline: Forest And Water

scenes.narration: People live there, and visitors come for fishing, even though the only road in goes through another country.
scenes.headline: Fishing In America

scenes.narration: A whole piece of America reached through Canada. But what about a whole country that sits inside another?
scenes.headline: A Country Inside One?

scenes.narration: If you enjoy strange places like these, do subscribe, because we post a new one every day.
scenes.headline: Like Strange Places?

scenes.narration: Number two. Lesotho is not a village or a town. It is a full country, and South Africa surrounds all of it.
scenes.headline: Number Two: Lesotho

scenes.narration: Whichever way you leave Lesotho by land, you end up in South Africa.
scenes.headline: Every Road Leads Out

scenes.narration: More than two million people live there, with their own king, their own flag and their own money, called the loti.
scenes.headline: Own King, Own Money

scenes.narration: It is one of only three countries in the world that are completely surrounded by one other country.
scenes.headline: One Of Only Three

scenes.narration: The other two are San Marino and the Vatican, which sit inside Italy, and both are tiny.
scenes.headline: San Marino, Vatican

scenes.narration: Lesotho is large enough to have mountains, ski slopes and snow, in the middle of southern Africa.
scenes.headline: Snow In Africa

scenes.narration: It is known as the Kingdom in the Sky, because every part of it is high above sea level.
scenes.headline: Kingdom In The Sky

scenes.narration: Its lowest point is about 1,400 metres up, which is the highest lowest point of any country in the world.
scenes.headline: Highest Lowest Point

scenes.narration: Because of this, almost everything Lesotho trades with the outside world has to pass through South Africa first.
scenes.headline: Everything Goes Through

scenes.narration: A country inside a country is strange. But India has something even stranger, and it ended only in 2015.
scenes.headline: Now: India's Strangest

scenes.narration: Number one. In Cooch Behar, in West Bengal, India and Bangladesh were mixed like a jigsaw.
scenes.headline: Number One: Cooch Behar

scenes.narration: Small patches of Indian land sat inside Bangladesh, and small patches of Bangladeshi land sat inside India.
scenes.headline: Patches In Both

scenes.narration: These patches were called chhitmahals, or enclaves. Some were a few acres, and some were a few villages.
scenes.headline: Called Chhitmahals

scenes.narration: One local story says the old kings of Cooch Behar and Rangpur played games and bet villages on them.
scenes.headline: A Game Of Kings

scenes.narration: Whatever the cause, the result was real: 162 patches of land that belonged to the wrong country.
scenes.headline: 162 Wrong-Side Patches

scenes.narration: In 2015, India gave Bangladesh 111 enclaves, and Bangladesh gave India 51.
scenes.headline: The 2015 Exchange

scenes.narration: Before that, people living in them were stuck. They were citizens of a country they could not easily reach.
scenes.headline: Stuck Citizens

scenes.narration: Many had no proper roads, schools or electricity from the government, because the land around them belonged to another country.
scenes.headline: No Roads, No Power

scenes.narration: Now for the strangest of all. One tiny plot called Dahala Khagrabari was a real-life Russian doll of countries.
scenes.headline: A Doll Of Countries

scenes.narration: It was Indian land, inside a Bangladeshi enclave, inside an Indian enclave, inside Bangladesh.
scenes.headline: Inside Inside Inside

scenes.narration: That is four layers of borders. It was the only one like this in the whole world.
scenes.headline: Only One In The World

scenes.narration: The plot was smaller than two acres, so a person could cross all of it in a short walk.
scenes.headline: Under Two Acres

scenes.narration: Just to walk from there to mainland India, you would have had to cross four borders.
scenes.headline: Four Borders To Walk

scenes.narration: At midnight on the thirty-first of July, 2015, the exchange began, and the enclaves changed hands.
scenes.headline: Midnight, 31 July 2015

scenes.narration: People waved flags, ate sweets and cheered, because many were finally getting a country that could reach them.
scenes.headline: Flags And Sweets

scenes.narration: Residents were given a choice, to stay where they were, or to move to the country they belonged to.
scenes.headline: Stay Or Move

scenes.narration: Some moved across the border into India, and many others chose to stay, and became citizens of Bangladesh.
scenes.headline: Some Moved, Many Stayed

scenes.narration: A line that took decades to fix was finally redrawn by a treaty, and the jigsaw map became a clean line.
scenes.headline: A Clean Line At Last

scenes.narration: So the strangest border on our list has already vanished. You can still see its odd shape in old maps.
scenes.headline: Gone, Still On Old Maps

scenes.narration: Let us count it back. Six, a sign that changes units. Five, a German village inside Switzerland.
scenes.headline: Counting It Back

scenes.narration: Four, a Spanish town in France. Three, American land you reach through Canada. Two, a country inside a country.
scenes.headline: Four, Three, Two

scenes.narration: One, an Indian plot inside three layers of borders. Every line on a map is a human decision.
scenes.headline: Lines Are Decisions

scenes.narration: Which brings you back to the start: your speed sign flips from miles to kilometres, and no road has moved.
scenes.headline: Same Road, New Units

scenes.narration: Next video: time zones that make no sense, including one in Nepal where your watch jumps by fifteen minutes.
scenes.headline: Next: Strange Time Zones
